title: More Than Numbers: Portraits of U.S. Citizens Detained by Immigration Agents
author: Nicole Foy
content:
The Department of Homeland Security says it’s not detaining Americans.

In written statements, it has said that “allegations that ICE is arresting and
deporting U.S. citizens is FALSE.”

It has said that “when individuals are briefly questioned under ‘reasonable
suspicion’ and are found to be U.S. citizens, they are immediately released.”
And it has said that “U.S. citizen agitators are only held while they actively
remain a safety threat to our officers and the public.”

But ProPublica has identified more than 500 citizens detained since President
Donald Trump returned to office.

They are not just numbers.

Among them is an elderly car wash owner whom agents repeatedly knocked to the
ground as they detained several of his workers. A 6-year-old whose mother says
still has nightmares after agents pointed guns at him and his siblings. A high
school senior who was detained after she tried to stop officers from
questioning her autistic younger brother. A dad who was held for several days
and missed his daughter’s third birthday.

Over the past year, several of these people shared the lingering effects of
what happened to them with ProPublica.

### Ana Michelle Ramirez Sanan

##### In their own neighborhood

![Three people stand close together against a teal wall decorated with
sketches and family photos. A young woman in a black shirt stands in the
center looking into the camera with her hands clasped in front of her. On the
left, an older woman wearing a red shirt and a black wrist brace rests her
head on the shoulder of the woman in the center. On the right, a person
wearing a black polo shirt leans their head against her other
shoulder.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/20260411-Maney-Citizens-Portrait-
Essay-008_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg?w=752)Photographed
at their home in a Boston suburb

> “We have so much trauma just from the 30 minutes we were held.”
>
> Ana Michelle Ramirez Sanan

In September 2025, Ana Michelle Ramirez Sanan learned that ICE agents had
intercepted members of her family as they drove one of her uncles to a court
hearing. Ramirez Sanan, then 17, said she rushed to the scene and discovered
agents had broken the car windows and pulled her two uncles, her mother and
her younger brother out. Video of the incident showed agents kicking and
slamming Ramirez Sanan’s mother to the ground and then twisting her arms to
handcuff her. Ramirez Sanan said she saw other agents questioning her brother
against a fence, threatening to arrest him if he couldn’t prove he had legal
status.

Both she and her brother are citizens.

“Him being a 13-year-old with autism, he doesn’t understand these things like
we do. He didn’t know what ‘a legal status’ is. He’s not able to tell them:
‘Yes, I have a legal status. I’m born here,’” Ramirez Sanan said. She said
that when she rushed toward her mom and brother, begging agents to let them
go, they detained her. “It was really scary thinking that they might have
taken us and deported us to Guatemala, where we don’t have anything.”

DHS said that its agents intercepted the car in order to detain the uncle who
was going to court that day, and that they “used the appropriate force
necessary.” He was facing charges of sexual assault on a child and remains in
ICE custody. He has pleaded not guilty.

As for Ramirez Sanan, her mother and her brother, they were released the day
of the incident. Her mother, who has lived in the United States for 20 years
and has a green card, was treated at a hospital for a concussion, bruising and
nerve damage in one of her arms.

DHS denies that they were ever detained.

“We have so much trauma just from the 30 minutes we were held,” said Ramirez
Sanan, who struggled with anxiety and depression after the incident. “I lost
my whole senior year fighting this. My brother isn’t the same either.”

### Andrea Velez

##### On her way to work

![A portrait of a woman with long dark hair standing outdoors in a park during
golden-hour light. She is wearing an oversized dark denim jacket over a blue
patterned sweater and light blue jeans, looking directly toward the camera,
against a soft-focus backdrop of green grass and
trees.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/20251229-Maney-
Citizens-Portrait-
Essay-023_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg?w=752)Photographed
in Los Angeles

In June 2025, Andrea Velez was dropped off at work at a shoe company in
downtown Los Angeles and inadvertently walked into an immigration raid on
street vendors. She said one of the masked agents rushed toward her, grabbed
her and slammed her to the pavement. Velez said she attempted to shield
herself with her work bag.

“Throughout the whole time, I kept saying I was a U.S. citizen,” Velez
recalled, saying that agents called her an “alleged U.S. citizen” even after
they checked her ID. “They kept saying how many ‘bodies they got’ that day.”

Velez said that she was detained for two days, and that she was denied an
opportunity to call family or a lawyer for most of that time. The government
charged Velez with assault. DHS said she “made physical contact” with agents
and tried to impede them. A judge ultimately dismissed the case.

After her arrest, Velez said she was so afraid of being detained again that
she worked remotely and avoided going outside.

### Quentin Williams

##### At the end of his school day as a teaching assistant

![A young man with dreadlocks sits on outdoor concrete steps next to a bright
blue handrail. He is dressed in a maroon T-shirt, olive green cargo shorts,
white crew socks and black sneakers, looking forward against a backdrop of
green grass, leafy trees and a blue fence.  ](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/20260711-Maney-Citizens-Portrait-
Essay-004_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg?w=752)Photographed
in Inver Grove Heights, Minnesota

In January, not long after immigration agents in Minneapolis had shot and
killed an American woman named Renee Good, Quentin Williams, a teaching
assistant at nearby Roosevelt High School, was guiding students toward buses
when more agents arrived outside his building.

Williams said that agents began confronting students and staff. At some point
during the commotion, he said, the agents threw him to the ground and choked
him so hard he couldn’t breathe.

“They didn’t even know what they were doing — just kind of being reckless
[with] assault rifles out and pepper-spraying staff after they took me down,”
Williams recalled.

Agents drove Williams to the Bishop Henry Whipple Federal Building, where they
detained him for several hours.

Later, then-Attorney General Pam Bondi published his photo on her social media
accounts, describing him as a “Minnesota rioter.” Federal authorities issued a
warrant for his arrest for assaulting officers. The charges against him were
eventually dismissed, and he’s filed a claim against the government for
damages over his arrest.

Williams said he’s still haunted by the idea that he came close to meeting the
same fates as Good and George Floyd, who was killed by a Minneapolis police
officer in 2020. “I didn’t leave the house for at least up to a week,” he
said. “I felt lucky to be alive.”

### Anabel Romero, John Carter, Juana Rodriguez and their children

##### Attending a horse race

In October 2025, some 200 federal agents and local police officers in armored
vehicles, a helicopter and on horseback conducted a raid on a racetrack in
Wilder, Idaho, and detained hundreds of people, including [dozens of
children](https://www.ktvb.com/article/news/investigations/7-investigates/idaho-
ice-raid-one-year-later-wilder-
operation/277-fe0c25d6-7896-4f9f-b88c-2de589e36dfe). Among them ProPublica
identified at least 30 U.S. citizens.

![A woman, a teenager and two young children pose together along a paved path
in an open park under a clear sky. The children stand in front — a boy in tan
sportswear and a girl in a purple shirt — with the woman and teenager standing
behind them resting hands on their shoulders.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/20260319-Maney-Citizen-
Kids-017_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg?w=752)Photographed
at a park in Meridian, Idaho

Anabel Romero had left her kids eating in the car while she went to look at
the horses. They were on opposite sides of the track when the raid began.

Romero said the agents wore camouflage and had their guns drawn. She had no
idea who they were. So she ran and tried to hide. “They didn’t identify
themselves,” Romero said. “I didn’t know who they were.”

She said unidentified officers tackled her, zip-tied her and threatened to
“fucking blow your head off.”

On the other side of the track, Romero’s 14-year-old daughter, SueHey Tello,
said officers surrounded their car, pointing guns at her brother, 6, and
sister, 8. When Tello refused to exit the car without her younger siblings,
agents pulled her so roughly out of the car that she fell, leaving bruises.
She said agents zip-tied her hands.

Romero and Tello said the agents refused to remove the zip ties for hours,
despite Tello’s age. The teenager said the incident has affected her view of
law enforcement. Her mother says that the 6-year-old still has nightmares.
Officers are meant “to keep us safe,” Tello said. “But yet they treated all of
us like that.”

![A bearded security guard wearing a black baseball cap that has the word
“security” on the front, glasses and a reflective high-visibility vest with
the word “security” along the bottom stands outdoors facing the camera with
his hands clasped. Flanking him are three other individuals also wearing
bright high-visibility vests, facing away toward an open landscape under a
clear sky.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/20260320-Maney-Citizen-
Kids-020_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg?w=752)Photographed
outside of La Catedral Arena in Wilder, Idaho, where they were detained

John Carter was working security at the track when the raid started. He had
brought his girlfriend and his two children along with him. He recalls
officers throwing a flash-bang near him and his son, and then the officers
detained them. “They cinched the zip ties down as tight as they could,” Carter
said. He said the officers also zip-tied his 14-year-old daughter but removed
the restraints when he complained.

Carter explained that he is active in the local Republican Party and a strong
supporter of law enforcement. But he said that what he saw officers doing that
day was wrong.

“Things are supposed to be done humanely and correctly,” he said. “This
wasn’t.”

![A woman with dark hair and glasses sits directly facing the camera on a dark
gray couch, hands resting in her lap. She wears a light-colored, floral-
patterned pullover jacket and blue jeans against a textured, light gray
wall.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/20260321-Maney-
Citizens-Portrait-
Essay-007_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg?w=752)Photographed
at her home in Caldwell, Idaho

The agents also detained Juana Rodriguez, who attended the event with her
family. She said that she was zip-tied beside her 3-year-old son, which left
her unable to pick him up and comfort him during the long hours they waited to
prove their citizenship. “He wanted me to hug him, to hold him,” Rodriguez
said. She and her son are both U.S. citizens and lead plaintiffs in an [ACLU
of Idaho lawsuit](https://www.aclu.org/cases/rodriguez-et-al-v-porter-et-al)
alleging the raid illegally targeted Latinos. ICE, the FBI and several Idaho
agencies have denied the charge and asked that the lawsuit be dismissed.  

DHS did not respond to any specific allegations made by Rodriguez, Romero,
Carter or their families. Instead, a spokesperson wrote in an email statement
that the raid successfully helped dismantle an illegal gambling operation, and
that ICE officers “didn’t zip tie, restrain or arrest any children.” The FBI
declined to comment to ProPublica but told local media no “young children”
were zip-tied. DHS, the FBI and multiple Idaho law enforcement agencies have
refused to share the number of U.S. citizens held that day.

### Amanda Trebach

##### Monitoring ICE operations

![A woman with short brown hair and forearm tattoos stands facing forward in
an empty, sunlit paved area wearing an olive green graphic T-shirt and dark
pants. In the background, a street leads toward an institutional complex
featuring watchtowers, perimeter fencing, utility poles and palm trees under a
bright blue sky.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/20260222-Maney-Citizens-Portrait-
Essay-023_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg?w=752)Photographed
outside Terminal Island in Los Angeles, where she was detained

> “I didn’t want to walk to my apartment by myself; I didn’t want to be out in
> the dark by myself.”
>
> Amanda Trebach

In August 2025, Amanda Trebach, a nurse and volunteer with an immigrant
advocacy organization, said she was monitoring ICE activities outside a
facility that the agency was using to stage operations when agents grabbed her
and pinned her to the ground, kneeling [on her neck and
back](https://www.propublica.org/article/videos-ice-dhs-immigration-agents-
using-chokeholds-citizens). They shoved her into the back of a van and held
her for several hours until taking her to a federal detention facility in Los
Angeles. She was not given the opportunity to speak with an attorney during
the 33 hours that she was in custody. She said agents took her phone and never
returned it.

DHS said Trebach was detained because she attempted to physically impede its
agents’ operations by jumping in front of moving vehicles, hitting their cars
with her protest signs and shouting obscenities at agents. She denies this.

She said that after the incident she felt paranoid that she was being
followed.

“I didn’t want to walk to my apartment by myself; I didn’t want to be out in
the dark by myself,” she said. “I didn’t know if they were going to come get
me.”

### George Retes

##### Driving to work

![A young man in a white T-shirt and patterned shorts sits in the open
driver’s-side door of a white car, looking directly toward the camera in warm
evening sunlight. Behind the vehicle, a vast green agricultural field
stretches out beneath a pale sky. ](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/20250919-Maney-Detained-
Citizens-129_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg?w=752)Photographed
in Carpinteria, California, where he was detained

George Retes, a U.S. Army veteran who served in Iraq, was driving into work at
a cannabis farm in July 2025 and arrived to find the place being raided by
immigration agents. Protesters had gathered outside the farm. He found himself
trapped between the agents and the protesters. The agents broke his car
window, pepper-sprayed him and pulled him out onto the ground. He was detained
for three days, missing his daughter’s third birthday. Retes said, agents
refused to explain why he’d been detained or to let him call relatives or a
lawyer.

When [ProPublica published](https://www.propublica.org/article/immigration-
dhs-american-citizens-arrested-detained-against-will) Retes’ story last year,
he said agents knew he was a citizen.  

“They didn’t care,” he recalled. “They still sent me away to jail.”

DHS officials made statements claiming Retes had assaulted their agents. But
he was never charged.

### Javier Ramirez

##### Working at his auto shop

![A bearded man stands outdoors between parked cars with his hands in his
pockets. He is wearing a light tan short-sleeved collared shirt, blue jeans
and brown shoes.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/20251229-Maney-Citizens-Portrait-
Essay-025_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg?w=752)Photographed
at his auto shop in Montebello, California, where he was detained

In June 2025, immigration agents conducted a raid on an auto shop owned by
Javier Ramirez and his family. He said agents swept him up as they were
detaining his workers. He recalled hearing one of the agents yell: “Hey, just
get him! He’s Mexican.” He said agents tackled him and one of them put a knee
on his face. He recalled hearing the agents boasting about the numbers of
immigrants they were detaining across the city that day, saying: “How many did
you get? I got 10, I got 15.” According to a lawsuit that Ramirez filed
against DHS, he said he was held in federal custody for four days and was
denied medication he needs for diabetes. DHS has not filed a response to the
lawsuit, but previously the agency said that Ramirez was arrested for
obstructing law enforcement, and that it never denied him medication.

### Jeane Wong

##### Monitoring ICE operations

![A woman with short blue-tinted gray hair leans against a blue wooden gate.
She is wearing a black graphic T-shirt featuring a green butterfly design and
dark trousers, with a large tortoise resting on the ground nearby next to lush
green foliage and flowering blue plumbago
bushes.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/20251212-Maney-
Citizens-Portrait-
Essay-009_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg?w=752)Photographed
at her home daycare center in San Diego

When Jeane “Bleu” Wong, an operator of a daycare center and activist, heard in
July 2025 that ICE agents had arrived at a nearby apartment complex, she
rushed to the scene to provide assistance to people who were being detained.
Agents detained her when she tried to remove one of their masks.

She was held in the [San Ysidro Port of
Entry](https://www.cbp.gov/about/contact/ports/san-ysidro-class-
california-2504), the largest and busiest land border crossing in the Western
Hemisphere, and later moved to a federal prison. Wong said that during her
time in custody she was strip-searched and shackled in chains that restricted
her from using the restroom. Federal authorities charged Wong with assaulting
a federal agent. She eventually pleaded guilty to a misdemeanor.

A little over a year later, Wong received a notice from the California
Department of Social Services that her license to care for children had been
revoked because of the assault. She and her wife are selling their home and
relocating outside of Southern California.

“We could totally fight, and I’d probably win,” she said. “But we don’t have
the money, time, energy.”

### Rafie Ollah Shouhed

##### Working at his car wash

![An older man with gray hair stands indoors leaning against a wooden railing,
wearing a pale yellow short-sleeved collared shirt — with a pen in his chest
pocket — and black trousers with a leather
belt.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/20251030-Maney-
Citizens-Portrait-
Essay-030_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg?w=752)Photographed
at his home in Tarzana, California

> “I was begging them, ‘Just let me breathe!’”
>
> Rafie Ollah Shouhed

Rafie Ollah Shouhed, 79, was born in Iran, moved to Los Angeles after the
Islamic Revolution and became a U.S. citizen. On Sept. 9, 2025, Shouhed, owner
of Valley Car Wash, watched with alarm as immigration agents stormed into his
business and attempted to detain his employees. He rushed outside to see what
was going on. Security video of the incident shows agents knocked Shouhed to
the ground repeatedly. He told agents that he had just had heart surgery.
“They were sitting on me,” he recalled. “I was begging them, ‘Just let me
breathe!’” He said in an ongoing lawsuit that the agents kept him handcuffed
for 12 hours and left him with injuries to his arm, elbows and ribs. Shouhed
said that he’s still receiving treatment for his injuries, and that he has
quit working. DHS said Shouhed was arrested for interfering with and
assaulting officers and did not answer questions about his lawsuit. He was
released without charges.  

### Leonardo Garcia Venegas

##### Working construction

![A man stands in an open grassy field looking toward the side with hands
tucked into the pockets of his blue jeans. He wears a gray long-sleeved
hoodie. In the background, a tall fence runs along the horizon beneath a clear
sky.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/20250911-Maney-
Detained-
Citizens-008_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg?w=752)Photographed
at a construction site in Foley, Alabama

Leonardo Garcia Venegas was laying concrete with his construction crew in
Alabama in May 2025 when immigration agents arrived at the site without a
warrant and began detaining his co-workers, including his brother. Garcia
Venegas pulled out his phone to film the agents. Videos he and other workers
recorded show agents approaching to arrest Garcia Venegas while he filmed,
tackling and arresting him while he yelled that he was a U.S. citizen. Garcia
Venegas said that he told the agents he had his REAL ID on him, but that they
dismissed the document as fake. They held him in handcuffs for an hour before
finally releasing him without charges. DHS said he was impeding officers.
After that first incident, immigration agents detained Garcia Venegas two more
times, each time ignoring statements and identification documents that prove
he is a U.S. citizen.

Garcia Venegas filed a lawsuit against DHS over its warrantless raids on
construction sites. DHS responded to the lawsuit, saying that its agents
didn’t need warrants to operate at construction sites because they’re open to
the public. The agency also said that brief stops like Garcia Venegas’ were
“reasonable.” Until the case is resolved, a judge ordered a temporary halt to
the operations.

“I just want to live in peace,” [he told ProPublica after his third
arrest](https://www.propublica.org/article/immigration-leo-garcia-venegas-
arrests-detentions-citizens-ice-dhs).

### Aliya Rahman

##### Driving to the doctor

![A woman stands in the middle of a crosswalk on a sunlit residential street,
using a forearm crutch on her left side and wearing a shoulder brace or
support across her upper chest. She wears a white blouse and dark trousers.
Leafy green trees, a pedestrian traffic signal and orange construction
barricades with a “sidewalk closed” sign are visible behind
her.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/20260711-Maney-
Citizens-Portrait-
Essay-006_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg?w=752)Photographed
in Minneapolis near the location she was detained

> “Nobody ever asked me for ID, my name or my citizenship.”
>
> Aliya Rahman

Aliya Rahman, who is autistic and disabled, was driving to a doctor’s
appointment in January when she reached an intersection where protesters were
confronting immigration officers. She said several agents swarmed her car and
yelled at her to move out of the way. They broke her window and pulled her
from the car.

“Nobody ever asked me for ID, my name or my citizenship,” Rahman said.

DHS said agents detained Rahman because she ignored their instructions. She
denied that, saying that she was confused and saw no way to move without
hitting someone.

She said agents then shackled her feet and held her in a detention cell at the
federal building. She passed out and awoke in a hospital room. She was
released without charges later that day.

### Jeyli Salguero

##### Sleeping in her bedroom

![A young woman stands in a bedroom between a tufted headboard and an
illuminated white vanity table, looking toward the camera. She wears a white
top with black polka dots, a black waistband accent and light blue
jeans.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/20260711-Maney-
Citizens-Portrait-
Essay-006_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95-1.jpg?w=752)Photographed
at her house in Oakdale, Minnesota, where she was detained

In January, Jeyli Salguero awoke when she heard someone banging on her door
and then the sound of the door breaking open. Federal agents, their guns
drawn, rushed inside and told her family they were looking for her brother.

“We told them yes he lived here, but he doesn’t live here anymore,” Salguero
said she told the agents. “They started getting a bit more angry and were
like, ‘Since you’re not collaborating, we’re gonna start checking your
status.’” An agent grabbed Salguero’s phone and ordered Salguero to face a
wall. In an ongoing lawsuit, Salguero has said that the agents entered the
home without a valid warrant. DHS said that agents were searching for a
fugitive, and that it has suspended the policy of entering homes without a
judicial warrant.

Her father has temporary protected status but had not received paperwork
showing that his status had been renewed. He was handcuffed and then detained
for a month. Salguero’s older sister, who was undocumented, was handcuffed and
deported to El Salvador. The rest of her family is now planning to sell their
home and move to El Salvador. “It’s been a mental toll — a very big mental
toll on all of us.”

### Juan Muñoz

##### Protesting the Broadview ICE Detention CenteR

![A man with a trimmed beard and mustache poses outdoors, dressed in a
charcoal suit, white dress shirt and blue patterned tie. He looks slightly
upward and away from the camera, positioned against a brick wall overgrown
with green climbing vines and orange flowers.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/20260709-Maney-Citizens-Portrait-
Essay-005_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg?w=752)Photographed
in Oak Park, Illinois

Juan Muñoz, an elected member of the Board of Trustees that governs Oak Park
Township outside of Chicago, was participating in an October protest outside
the Broadview ICE Detention Center when he said that he was knocked to the
ground by the commander of the Border Patrol. “When I looked up,” Muñoz
recalled, “it was Commander Greg Bovino who was standing over me.” In
depositions, Bovino denied tackling Muñoz, saying videos of the arrests showed
no “reportable uses of force.”

Muñoz said agents knocked away his phone and zip-tied his hands. “Every agent
that I encountered, I told the same thing, ‘I’m an elected official.’ No
response.”

Muñoz was held inside of the detention center for eight hours before agents
dropped him off at a gas station, without explaining why he’d been held. “They
were over capacity, keeping people for way longer than that facility was
intended for,” he recalled about the detention center. “It was filthy. They
don’t have proper hygiene products or are able to feed people properly,” Muñoz
said. DHS did not comment on his specific detention. But, referring to Muñoz
and other protesters detained with him, it posted a comment on social media,
saying, “We will NOT allow violent activists to lay hands on our law
enforcement.”

### Jessie Fuentes

##### Responding to ICE in a hospital

![A woman in a black T-shirt and light gray trousers leans against the door of
a storefront office featuring signage for Chicago Alderperson Jessie Fuentes
and the Chicago city seal.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/20260708-Maney-Citizens-Portrait-
Essay-016_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg?w=752)Photographed
at her office in Chicago

In October 2025, Chicago Alderperson Jessie Fuentes said she rushed to a local
emergency room because she’d been told that ICE agents had been spotted
inside. She identified herself to the agents as an elected official and began
asking them whether they’d obtained a warrant. Video taken of the incident
shows that agents grabbed and handcuffed her. Fuentes was held for 15 minutes,
during which time members of her staff posted the video online and her
supporters gathered outside the hospital to demand her release. DHS, in a
written statement, told ProPublica that Fuentes was put in “handcuffs but
NEVER placed under arrest.”

“These individuals are operating above the law,” Fuentes said. “They’re
operating with impunity.”

### Caitlin Arwen

##### Monitoring ICE operations

![A woman wearing a baseball cap, an open plaid collared shirt over a purple
top and brown flared trousers stands in the center of a quiet paved
neighborhood street. She faces forward with hands clasped, flanked by green
lawns, a roadside mailbox and mature trees stretching along the road behind
her.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/20260710-Maney-
Citizens-Portrait-
Essay-022_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg?w=752)Photographed
in Maple Park, Illinois, where she was detained

Caitlin Arwen was scrolling through a Facebook group for moms in October when
she noticed a shared post that said immigration agents were detaining people
in her town, which is about an hour’s drive outside of Chicago. Later that day
she saw some of the vehicles that had been posted on Facebook and began
following them, honking her horn to alert residents of their presence. One of
the vehicles slammed on its brakes. U.S. marshals who were working with ICE
surrounded her car, broke her window and pulled her out.

“They threw me on the broken glass, and they were all on top of me. I couldn’t
breathe,” she recalled. Arwen estimates she was kept handcuffed face down on
broken glass for roughly 35 minutes. “They taunted me, took photos of me,
called me names, berated me and acted like I was somehow deserving of this.”
DHS referred questions about Arwen’s arrest to the U.S. Marshals Service. A
spokesperson for the service said Arwen’s arrest was a “task force arrest” and
declined further comment.

Arwen was taken to a hospital, where marshals handcuffed her to the bed. After
she was discharged, agents shackled her and moved her to a DHS detention
facility, where she was not allowed to contact a lawyer or anyone else for
help. “I didn’t have access to water or food the whole time,” said Arwen,
adding that she was held for several hours. “Nobody showed me their badge all
day. No one identified themselves. No one once read me my Miranda rights.”

Though federal officials declined to prosecute Arwen, state authorities
charged her with traffic violations and obstruction of law enforcement. She
has pleaded not guilty.
